title: Simon's problem: Theta(2^(n/2)) classical queries vs O(n) quantum queries
problem_statement: Given oracle access to f: {0,1}^n -> {0,1}^n with the promise that there is a nonzero s such that f(x) = f(y) iff y = x or y = x XOR s, find s.

input.parameter: n = number of input bits of f.
input.size_measure: Query model: cost is the number of oracle calls. The harness materialises the 2^n-entry table only so that the oracle can be simulated.

algorithms.name: classical collision search
algorithms.idea: Query distinct random points until two values collide; the XOR of the colliding inputs is s.
algorithms.pseudocode: for x in random permutation: if f(x) seen at x': return x XOR x'
algorithms.time_complexity: Theta(2^(n/2)) queries expected: exactly 2^N / binom(N, N/2) with N = 2^n, which lies strictly between sqrt(pi N / 2) and sqrt(pi N / 2) e^(1/(3N)) (birthday law; PROOFS.md §2); at most 2^(n-1) + 1
algorithms.space_complexity: Theta(2^(n/2)) stored values in expectation (at most 2^(n-1)), plus the list of 2^n indices that the random order is drawn into (PROOFS.md §2)
algorithms.correctness: Under the promise, f(x) = f(x') with x != x' implies x' = x XOR s (PROOFS.md §2).

algorithms.name: Simon's quantum algorithm
algorithms.idea: Each round (Hadamard, one query, Hadamard, measure) yields a uniformly random y with y.s = 0. About n rounds give n-1 independent equations, which Gaussian elimination over GF(2) solves for s.
algorithms.time_complexity: O(n) queries: the expected number of rounds is E(n) = sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 1/(1 - 2^(-j)) = n - 1 + sum_{j=1}^{n-1} 1/(2^j - 1) < n + 0.6067 (the limit constant is the Erdős-Borwein constant 1.60669...; PROOFS.md §5); plus O(n^3) expected bit operations of classical post-processing (O(n^2) per round)
algorithms.correctness: After measuring the output register the input register is (|x0> + |x0 XOR s>)/sqrt(2); after H^n, the amplitude of y is proportional to 1 + (-1)^(y.s), so only y with y.s = 0 occur, uniformly, in exact arithmetic (PROOFS.md §3; the floating-point simulation agrees up to rounding, PROOFS.md preamble); n - 1 linearly independent such y span {y : y.s = 0}, and the elimination returns its unique nonzero orthogonal vector s (PROOFS.md §4). Credit: Simon 1997.

lower_bounds.bound: more than sqrt((2^(n+1) - 6)/3) queries for success probability at least 1/2 on every input (n >= 2): Omega(2^(n/2)) queries for bounded error
lower_bounds.source: Proved in this entry (PROOFS.md §6): for s uniform and random labels, after collision-free queries s is uniform on the nonzero values not excluded by the queried pairs, so q queries succeed with probability at most (C + 1)/(2^n - 1 - C), C = q(q - 1)/2. Credit: Simon 1997

relationship: EXPONENTIAL separation in the query model: Omega(2^(n/2)) classical queries vs O(n) quantum queries (fewer than n + 0.61 in expectation), both sides proved in PROOFS.md (§5, §6; credit: Simon 1997). The relation to Shor's factoring algorithm is background.

background.statement: Simon's algorithm inspired Shor's factoring and discrete-logarithm algorithms.
background.source: Shor 1997, introduction ('Simon's algorithm inspired the work presented in this paper'; read in arXiv quant-ph/9508027v2)

sources.title: On the power of quantum computation
Polynomial-Time Algorithms for Prime Factorization and Discrete Logarithms on a Quantum Computer

verification.method: V1: both algorithms return s, independently checked against the promise structure of the table, for n = 1, ..., 6, 8, 10 (quantum, simulated exactly with lib/qsim.py using deferred measurement of the output register) and also 16 (classical). V2 measures QUERY COUNTS reported through lib.qsim.Oracle, averaged over random instances: classical fits 2^(n/2) and quantum fits n. Before the revision below, quantum counts were averaged over 40 instances per n for n = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 10, where the exact expectation E(n) (see time_complexity) has log-log slope 1.019 against n (1.013 over every n = 2..10). Separately, the simulator's mean query count was compared with E(n) on 1500-4000 instances per n for n = 2, 3, 4, 6, 8: all within 1.3 standard errors (RESEARCH_LOG.md, 2026-10-06). Simulation time is exponential in n and is not the claim. Revised 2026-10-06 (RL-056): quantum n_values 3, 4, 6, 8, 10 with 100 instances per n (n = 2 dropped: its geometric spread dominated the fit, deviation analysis F5); the exact expectation E(n) has log-log slope 0.9573 against n over these values. Rivals: the quantum counts must reject 2^(n/2), the classical counts must reject n. Proofs: PROOFS.md proves every claim of this entry (the count per round, the correctness and expected queries of both algorithms, the distribution of one quantum round, the post-processing, and the classical lower bound) and names the deterministic checks of each (tests/test_proofs_query.py, the experiment and count-check scripts).

caveats: A separation relative to an oracle; it does not by itself imply BQP != BPP for explicit problems. The simulation never materialises the output register: lib.qsim.Oracle.apply_xor_and_measure_output samples the measured output value and collapses the input register, which is exact because the algorithm never touches the output register again (PROOFS.md §3).
notes: An exponential quantum-classical query separation, both sides proved in PROOFS.md; for its relation to Shor's algorithm see background (and staging/integer-factoring, staging/discrete-logarithm).
